section.title: Optional: why one small scale works everywhere
section.p: This investigation supplies fuller justifications for facts stated for use in Chapters 13, 17 and 19. It is optional throughout. The four folded exercises form a sequence; each names its earlier optional prerequisites. Their solutions are complete arguments using the explicitly supplied completeness fact below, unlike the shorter proof sketches elsewhere in this appendix.

aside.title: Optional: the completeness fact and vocabulary for this investigation
aside.p: We supply the nested-interval fact: decreasing nonempty closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to zero have exactly one common point. Applying this in each coordinate gives the same result for nested closed boxes whose side lengths tend to zero. This fact expresses completeness of the real numbers; we do not prove completeness here.

A sequence is a list x_1,x_2,\ldots. A subsequence x_{n_1},x_{n_2},\ldots selects terms with strictly increasing indices. Convergence to x means that eventually all selected terms are within every prescribed positive distance of x. An open set contains a small open ball around each of its points; a set is closed when its complement is open. A bounded set lies in a finite box. The diameter of a box with side lengths at most \ell in \mathbb R^n is at most \sqrt n\,\ell.

statement.p: Use the supplied nested-box fact in . Given a sequence in a nonempty closed bounded set K\subseteq\mathbb R^n, enclose it in a closed box. Bisect every side and retain a subbox containing infinitely many terms (counted by their indices). Repeat. Choose one term in the kth box with index larger than every previously selected index. Show that these selected terms converge to the common point of the boxes. Why must that point belong to K?

solution.p: At each stage finitely many subboxes cover the previous box. If each held only finitely many indices, their union would too, a contradiction. Thus the construction continues, and infinitely many available indices permit the increasing selection. If the initial longest side is L, the kth box has diameter at most \sqrt n L/2^k. Completeness supplies a common point x, and the distance from the selected term to x is at most that diameter, hence tends to zero. If x\notin K, the open complement contains a ball about x disjoint from K; convergence would eventually put selected terms of K in that ball. Thus x\in K.

exercise.title: Optional: from continuity to one common distance bound

statement.p: This exercise uses . A continuous map f:K\to\mathbb R^m on a closed bounded set is uniformly continuous if, for every \varepsilon>0, there is \delta>0 such that \|f(x)-f(y)\|<\varepsilon whenever x,y\in K and \|x-y\|<\delta. Assume this fails. Explain why some fixed \varepsilon_0>0 admits points x_k,y_k\in K with \|x_k-y_k\|<1/k but output distance at least \varepsilon_0. Extract a convergent subsequence of x_k and use continuity to reach a contradiction.

solution.p: Failure of the stated quantifiers gives such a fixed error and pairs for every allowed distance 1/k. The preceding exercise gives x_{k_j}\to x\in K. The triangle inequality gives \|y_{k_j}-x\|\le1/k_j+\|x_{k_j}-x\|\to0. Continuity at x makes both output sequences tend to f(x), so their difference tends to zero, contradicting the fixed lower bound. The empty-set case is immediate. This also proves the result for a continuous vector-valued map, since only distances were used.

exercise.title: Optional: a uniform radius for an open cover

statement.p: This exercise uses . An open cover of K is a collection of open sets whose union contains K. Prove that if K is closed and bounded, some \eta>0 has this property: for every x\in K, the ball B(x,\eta) lies in one member of the cover. If this fails, choose bad centers for radii 1/k and extract a convergent subsequence. Then enclose K in a finite grid with cell diameter less than \eta, choose a point of K in each occupied cell, and deduce that finitely many members cover K.

solution.p: Suppose no common radius works, and choose x_k\in K such that B(x_k,1/k) lies in no member. Pass to x_{k_j}\to x\in K. One covering set U contains x, so B(x,r)\subseteq U for some r>0. Eventually \|x_{k_j}-x\|+1/k_j<r, so B(x_{k_j},1/k_j)\subseteq U, a contradiction. Choose a grid of side length less than \eta/\sqrt n in a bounding box. There are finitely many cells. Every point in an occupied cell is within \eta of its selected point, so the associated cover member contains that cell. These finitely many members cover K. If K is empty, the empty subcollection suffices. Notice that we established the common scale before extracting the finite cover; merely naming a finite cover would not prove the scale assertion.

exercise.title: Optional: subdividing paths and parameter rectangles

statement.p: This exercise uses directly. Let P be a closed bounded interval or rectangle and H:P\to D continuous, where D is open. Show that some \delta>0 ensures that every nonempty closed cell Q\subseteq P of diameter less than \delta has image in an open ball contained in D. If this fails, choose cells of diameter less than 1/k and one point in each; extract a subsequence and use continuity at its limit. Explain why the same argument controls every point in each small cell.

solution.p: Choose failing cells Q_k and points u_k\in Q_k. A subsequence tends to u\in P. Since D is open, B(H(u),r)\subseteq D for some r>0. Continuity relative to P gives \eta>0 such that \|H(v)-H(u)\|<r for v\in P within \eta of u. For every v\in Q_{k_j}, \|v-u\|\le\operatorname{diam}(Q_{k_j})+\|u_{k_j}-u\| <1/k_j+\|u_{k_j}-u\|. Eventually this is less than \eta, independently of the chosen v. The entire image then lies in B(H(u),r), contradicting failure. A grid with side lengths below \delta/\sqrt n, where n=1 or 2, has the required diameter bound. This proves the supplied path theorem in and the rectangle fact used in .
